analysis.investment_thesis: DOMS is a genuinely good business — ROCE of 26.2%, ROE of 22.3%, low debt, a recognizable consumer brand in Indian stationery, and a FILA partnership for premiumization — but at P/E 65x and EV/EBITDA of 39x, you are paying a full quality premium with virtually no margin of safety. The business deserves respect; the price does not.
key_strengths: ROCE of 26.2% and ROE of 22.3% meet and exceed my 20% threshold — this is the only stock in this batch with genuinely excellent capital returns
Operating margin expanded from 11.6% (FY20) to 13.7% (FY25) at scale, demonstrating real operating leverage in a branded consumer goods business
Strong promoter alignment at 70.4% and very low D/E of 0.14 — management has skin in the game and has not over-leveraged to fund growth
key_risks: Valuation of P/E 65x and EV/EBITDA 39x on a business generating INR 214 Cr net profit requires flawless execution for years — any growth disappointment will be punished severely
Free cash flow was negative in FY25 (-INR 26 Cr) and FY20 (-19 Cr) as capex (INR 213 Cr in FY25) consumes OCF; the business is investment-heavy during expansion
Entry into baby diapers/wet wipes is a strategic red flag — diversification away from core stationery competency into a commoditized, heavily competitive FMCG category
red_flags: At INR 14,517 Cr market cap on INR 1,913 Cr revenue, the stock is priced at 6.5x sales — any deceleration from the 24% revenue CAGR will compress the multiple rapidly
CWIP of INR 101 Cr jumped significantly in FY25, signaling ongoing heavy investment — FCF may remain pressured for 1-2 more years
analysis.detailed_analysis:
DOMS is the closest thing in this batch to a quality compounder. The stationery market in India is underpenetrated relative to global peers, and DOMS has systematically built brand recognition through schools and art supply channels. The FILA joint venture provides access to a premium European brand and technology, differentiating DOMS from domestic competitors. The financial metrics — 26% ROCE, expanding margins, low leverage, consistent OCF — are the hallmarks of a well-run consumer franchise.

However, applying my valuation discipline: I am being asked to pay 65x earnings for a business that earns INR 214 Cr on INR 14,517 Cr of market cap. The earnings yield is 1.5%. Even if DOMS compounds profits at 25% annually for 5 years, I'm still buying at ~21x FY30 earnings today — fair, but not cheap. Munger's rule is 'a great business at a fair price'; DOMS qualifies on quality but not on price. I'd watch closely at 40-45x forward P/E for a better entry.
